articles.title: Growing up between languages
articles.description: Growing up, the language I spoke depended on where I was. At school, it was English. But at home, conversations occurred in two different worlds: Mandarin and Fuzhounese with my parents and grandparents; and English with my brother and sister. Sometimes, one conversation occurred in three languages. My parents could ask me a question in Mandarin, and I would respond in a mix of Fuzhounese and English without thinking twice. At dinner time, my parents made a rule that we could only speak Mandarin and Fuzhounese. My grandparents didn't understand English, and my parents didn't want them to be left out of the hectic conversations my siblings and I had. Each time we would speak English at the dinner table, my parents joked that we were talking about our grandparents, and we would immediately counter that we were not, in Fuzhounese. However, as I got older, I started to notice the gaps between my speech. There were words I understood in one language, but didn't know how to translate into another. There were also moments when I knew what I wanted to say, but didn't know the right words to say it. Very often, I start my sentences in Fuzhounese, only to discover that I can't find the words to finish the other half of my sentence. It's strange. On other occasions, I would completely understand what my parents were saying but found it difficult to convey my own thoughts. Over the years, my Mandarin has gotten rusty because I haven't used it as much. Now at Hopkins, those gaps have become more apparent. Whenever I hear other people speak Mandarin on campus, it makes me want to become more fluent again. Back home, switching between three languages was normal. But hearing other students speaking in complete sentences in solely Mandarin made me realize how much I've forgotten. Right now, my 1,405 day Duolingo streak is helping me. Although it is only for a few minutes every day, I am slowly building up my vocabulary and comprehension skills. I've also started to talk with my other Chinese friends in Mandarin rather than English, helping me gain confidence in expressing myself in a language that has slowly slipped away from me. Aside from Duolingo, I have started to listen intently to Mandopop and watching Chinese movies. From idioms to slang and expressions, each time I pick up a new word or phrase that I wouldn't normally hear when talking with my parents in day-to-day conversations. Switching languages has always been the way I communicate, and sometimes it has been the only way to communicate, especially with family members like my grandparents who don't speak English. I am from Fuzhou, China; and each time I visit, hearing locals speak in a language I grew up with gives me a sense of belonging. Being born in Delaware, English connects me with the place I grew up. Being Chinese, Mandarin also connects me with my heritage and culture. Although I can't speak each language perfectly, all of them together shape me into who I am. Raymond Chen is a freshman from Middletown, De. majoring in Biomedical Engineering.

articles.title: Hopkins and the inner child
articles.description: The phrase is "gas-powered nose hair trimmer." The two guys trying to guess are playing newscasters, and they look at each other with direct and purposeful glances while the girl miming sticks her finger in her nose. "Ladies and gentlemen, call this number for a free nose hair clipper!" reels the first newscaster. "A free nose hair shaver! A free nose hair…trimmer!" An unseen crowd applauds; laughs as the girl begins to swish her hand near her behind and cover her nose. "Republicans?" asks a second voice. But I am distracted from the joke by the timbre of the words. I feel like I've heard this voice before. After a moment I realize that this second guy has the same voice that one of the current Buttered Niblets, the Hopkins improv comedy group, so distinctively possesses - deep, nasally, prodigiously middle-aged, swelling with images of belts and decks. And it must be the voice of the Niblet soul, for the guy on my screen is also a Niblet, and he speaks now from their performance at O-week, 1995. And from the voice, and from the dim corners of the 31-year-old theatre, I glimpse a true symbol of the spontaneous and joyous at Hopkins. A symbol of the inner child at Hopkins. I have come to search for the inner child here at Hopkins, because I am curious about how that fragile part of us, that lies beyond the elite academics and the $250 million student centers, is doing. There is, of course, some tension in the relationship between the school and its inner child. You will agree with me there, regardless of your definition of the term: Hopkins is stressful, and remember, our inner children still have Twenty One Pilots ringing in their ears from 2015. But how exactly does the stress of Hopkins affect the inner child? What exactly do the Buttered Niblets have to teach us? "I knew you were a freshman because you still have whimsy," a girl told me, freshman year. What exactly does that mean? Perhaps - now a junior, mature and un-whimsical as a stone - I may deduce the answer. First, we must remember that the inner child, though elusive, is not a complex being. That much is apparent in their downy, sun-drenched hair, in fourth and fifth of their friendship bracelets, in each pixel of Thomas the Tank Engine's disturbed face on their TV. As such, the old and simple things of our generation - Four Square, Bob's Burgers, Counter-Strike: Global Offensive, and Fortnite - are reliably rejuvenating. It would seem that all we need is time and a little nostalgia, and that the function, the difficulty, of Hopkins, is just to take away the time. And this is not a bad first start. Not only does Hopkins eat time through homework and all the various extras, but it often salivates at the edge of our free time, too, whispering about "a deeper understanding." It is here that the Hopkins perspective that any coffee shop or park bench would be better enjoyed with a MacBook and a Celsius finds its origin. But finding the inner child does not always require finding time. It is still possible to reconnect with our inner children on a tight schedule: look at the Niblets. Sure, they practice three hours a week (at least according to the official Buttered Niblets Constitution), but on stage, they demonstrate over and over that immediate reconnection is possible; that there exist nose-hair trimmers and Republicans floating in the Platonic aether, waiting to be summoned. The Niblets offer a second model of rejuvenation: make improv comedy of your life. Repurpose an object, reinvent a game, play. It is not always necessary, they tell us, to sit down at the beginning of the week and choose which hours to sacrifice to free time. Simply drop whatever you're doing, act on a few ridiculous ideas, and laugh at the exponential chaos. Furthermore, there are other factors equally, if not more, important than time. Like wonder. We Hopkins students can struggle with wonder, for good reason: one does not particularly want to wonder during a test, or while doing their homework at an early hour, and these two activities comprise a large part of each day. Wondering about whether or not one's GPA is good enough for med school: also not so enjoyable. So a great desire for certainty settles over campus. But one of the defining joys of childhood is that nothing is certain. For all of your mental pictures to be totally overexposed; to live amongst more light than understanding; to glimpse pure burning possibility in the parking lot beyond your elementary school fence - that is the joy, that is the wonder. How can we partake? Kids wonder because they are yet to recognize that a parking lot is a parking lot, the whole day through. We might love, at times, to have the same ignorance, but it's not that easy. But there is so much else we don't know. Academically, for one - isn't the previous sentence our exact sentiment before any test? If we could look above the pressure, what might we see? I admit doing this is difficult. Two years of intake has really strained my love for math, my primary major. But I know I still enjoy the subject, because I get a kick out of the rare times I get to do math just for fun, outside my classes. What's the last time you worked on something in your field just for fun, outside of the grades/applications/career context? Outside of the desire for certainty? Could it be that we are all just one good walk around Druid Hill, discussing academics, away from that other promise of college: to use academics to endow honest-to-god bearded, balding adults with a childlike capacity for wonder? Also, there is much we don't know about our surroundings. Who's to say they really know this 225-year-old campus? Is there not some pocket of ignorance into which Aureliano Buendía could still stumble and discover ice? Some remaining mystery among these 140 acres that has not yet been dug up or optimized or reconstructed? Is it a case of gems in Olin Hall? Is it an obscure, possibly biohazardous corner of the Wyman Park building? Is it the steam tunnels? (Is it? Is the key to wonder to be the first student past than O-week to go down there?) The Merrick Barn, the Evergreen Library, the inner clocktower, the Bloomberg observatory! All may work, given zero stress. But is there one that works a little better, takes us a little higher? I like the Baltimore Museum of Art. Once, I found an obscure hallway there, on my way down to the first-floor bathrooms. This hallway - it was covered, walls, ceiling, and floor, in beautiful, carved dark wood. Money and taste are a hell of a combination. I went down this hallway to the bathrooms, this marbled, stained cocoon, and I felt everything else disappear. And finally, zoom out: what about Baltimore in general? Who's to say they really know this 297-year-old city? We already know that Baltimore is 80 square miles of the weird, the eclectic, the gorgeous, the ugly, the charming and the dysfunctional, often in the same place. But what that really means is that wonder - an experience with causes as diverse as childhoods - is available here to anybody. On the one hand, you have last July 4: 20,000 people swarming the Inner Harbor, all the songs playing at once and the red-white-and-blue hairstyles and what I could swear were people lighting miniature fireworks upside down - I can guarantee that then I entered the tricolored haze of zero understanding. And on the other hand, you have Kitsch Cafe, the one on University Parkway, that the Carlyle sits on top of. You already know what Kitsch looks like: stickers and avocados everywhere. But I also like what the people look like there. They wear flannels and Ravens tees and some wear beads. Their dogs take turns drinking from the bowl outside. And in the décor, but especially in the people, there is a groundedness, a domesticity that I have missed. It is funny but fitting; even in the green hair, I find that I can feel the earth again. It is the smallness of childhood wonder, the intimacy with the world. These poor children! We deny them; believe that Hopkins is only for work. We forget them; imagine we are pre-everything. And we have a skepticism of them, too. Their eyes, in ours, are far too wide - they expect so much of the world, and they never put in the work! How weak! Personally, I can still see him - stuck in his own protracted adolescence, spending hours trying to improvise the last undiscovered gem of romantic pianism. I can still smell the AMR I showers on his stupid crinkled hair. And yet there were many times when I was happy. Weren't there many times when we were happy? "The grasses of Gilman quad grow long and languid," whispers the Niblet soul. "Strange bells begin to rustle. The sun has almost scaled the clocktower. It is high time to make a change!" Jeff Warner is a junior majoring in Mathematics and English from Northampton, Mass.

articles.title: Loving a place I no longer belong to
articles.description: "I want to go home." Those who know me probably heard this line a lot during my first two weeks of college. By home, I meant California, not my dorm. I thought the hardest part of leaving home would mostly mean getting used to a new place, new classes and new people. I didn't quite expect how much I am losing touch with a life at home that was still going on without me. Now, 2,867 miles away from home, I often sit in my dorm and call friends who used to know me almost as well as I knew myself. We talk about school, how calculus is roasting both of us and how physics makes no sense. Then, almost inevitably, I ask, "How is California?" I find it strange that I now refer to the place I grew up in by its proper name instead of simply calling it home. I used to know what was happening there without having to ask. Now, I have to specify exactly where I mean, as if California is somewhere I need to check in rather than somewhere I belong. As my friends tell me about their lives, I hear names I don't recognize. They talk about people I have never met, inside jokes I don't understand and memories I wasn't there to make. I look through the photos they send me, trying to catch up on a life that used to also be mine. I am happy that they are enjoying college, but there is something strange about watching everyone move forward from so far away. I still know these people. I still care about them. Yet, for the first time, I am beginning to feel like an outsider in their lives. I have started noticing the other little things, too. My parents have quietly switched from asking, "When will you be home?" to "When will you visit?" I don't remember when that changed. Maybe they have been asking this for a while, and I am only noticing it now. But the word "visit" feels different. A "visit" is temporary. It means coming back for a little while and leaving again. My sister now calls to update me about her life. Half the time, though, I am too tired to process everything she tells me, or I have no idea what is going on at her high school. She talks about people I have never met, and their names don't correspond to faces in my mind. After all, I can no longer pick her up from school and see the faces of the people she is ranting about. Her life keeps moving forward, but now just without me. I wonder how many moments I will miss, how many people will become important to her whom I will only ever know by name. The strange thing is that despite missing a life in California, I am building a life here, too. I have classes to complain about, people to meet and experiences my friends back home will never fully understand. But whenever I call my friends, I still want to know what I have missed, as if keeping up with every detail could keep me from falling behind. I want my life here to move forward, but I am not quite ready for my life there to move on without me. I used to not be fully able to comprehend the concept that you can one day watch the people you love the most build lives without you. But I guess now I do. I don't know what it will feel like when I return. My friends will have new stories, my sister will have new people to tell me about, and I will have experiences of my own that they weren't there to witness. I still want to go home. I just hope that when I do, it will feel like coming home. Suya Fang is a freshman majoring in Engineering Mechanics and Neuroscience from Los Altos, Calif.

articles.title: My Little Pony, My Little Escape
articles.description: If there is an afterlife, I want to be a My Little Pony character. I want a pastel-colored flowy mane, beautiful wings that take me places, and a cutie mark (a special symbol on a flank that represents a unique talent, passion, or purpose in life) - for the latter, I don't even know what it would show. I've been rewatching My Little Pony very intermittently for the past few years. I would rather watch my colorful pony show preach their friendship lessons and break into song than scroll through Love Island memes on TikTok. It's not really nostalgic: in fact, I feel like I've been more connected to it in my older years. During my childhood summers in China, I had only seen Equestria Girls, the spin-off franchise of My Little Pony completely in Chinese, where they fight the villainous dragons in their human form (The Dazzlings from Rainbow Rocks) by singing about how friendship is magic; I loved collecting the figurines from McDonald's Happy Meals. Maybe that's why revisiting My Little Pony feels less like returning to my childhood and more like meeting a younger version of myself for the first time, or even creating a new younger version of myself (age regression much?). As I find myself returning to it voluntarily, I understand the jokes differently, I relate way too much to Twilight Sparkle and Pinkie Pie's crashouts, I recognize parts of myself in the characters that I never consciously related to back then and I actually like Applejack. Growing up means constantly outgrowing things: friendships, cringey phases, niche interests and versions of yourself you once thought you'd be forever. We're told to move forward, mature and leave childish things behind. Sometimes, going back is its own kind of growing up. You get to experience them again through a new and older version of yourself without worrying about whether it's childish or cringe or something you should've grown out of by now. And maybe you realize you never really outgrew them at all. You just needed to grow into them. Honestly, I do have better things to do. I have midterms to study for, and I have a lot of things that I should have figured out as a legal adult. Sometimes, I just want to watch cartoon ponies make dumb decisions that turn into a valuable friendship lesson rather than do anything productive. I don't see it as a bad thing. There's something comforting being in a little corner of a world where I can exist and enjoy something without justifying why and never asking anything from me. I spend so much time worrying about who I'm eventually supposed to become that I forget I'm allowed to enjoy who I am right now. As childish as it sounds, I want my wings. I want to fly around some fictional land where I don't have to have everything figured out, including which cutie mark I'd have if I were a pony. I know I can't actually become a pony, and I know watching a children's cartoon won't solve any of my problems. For now, I think it's enough to simply have a comfort show. Even though I am getting old, I would rather not rush the parts of being young that I still get to enjoy. Grace Wang is a junior from Tuscaloosa, Ala. majoring in Neuroscience and Molecular and Cellular Biology.

articles.title: Anna Durbin speaks on a new understanding of infection models
articles.description: Most clinical trials ask how diseases can be fought. But what if the answer to this question relies on understanding how the disease begins and progresses? This is what Dr. Anna Durbin, Professor of International Health at the School of Public Health, spoke about in her talk "The Use of Controlled Human Infection Models to Evaluate Countermeasures for Dengue and Zika Virus" in the Molecular Microbiology and Immunology Department Seminar on Thursday, Oct. 29. Durbin opened her talk by defining what a controlled human infection model (CHIM) is. "We infect people with pathogens, and we follow the course of disease. And we do this for different reasons; we can do this to study… what the kinetics of an infection, for instance a viral infection, is, what the clinical manifestations are," she explained. "We typically use these in the evaluation of countermeasures such as vaccines and therapeutics." "We monitor these participants very closely. And I think the important part of a controlled human infection model is the word 'controlled,' because we control everything; we control the dose, we control the way that the pathogen is administered, we control how long it's been from, for instance, vaccination to challenge," she said. Durbin further categorized CHIMs into two different types: the disease model and the infection model. The disease model typically involves enteric pathogens - microbes that infect the gastrointestinal tract such as Salmonella or Shigella - and assesses the severity of disease in patients. This entails tracking symptoms and assigning disease scores. The infection model, on the other hand, is not focused on disease progression. Rather, it looks at the collection of the pathogen of interest at different times throughout an infection to understand when the microbe reaches certain concentrations within the host. She continued to explain that CHIMs are particularly useful to establish the efficacy of a therapeutic and a correlate of protection before bringing it to an expensive clinical trial stage. Historically, some vaccine candidates brought to the clinical trial stage have shown evidence of efficacy in mice or other animal models, but are ineffective when used in humans. A CHIM can ensure only therapies showing promising results are moved to the costly trial stage or can bypass trial stages altogether. She then transitioned into sharing some of the work done in her lab to develop a controlled human infection model for dengue, noting that the lack of adequate animal models for this infection make it a great candidate for work in humans. Durbin's group developed their CHIM using a virus strain that was originally developed for a live attenuated vaccine but was ultimately abandoned. They infected participants with 1000 infectious viral particles and collected blood samples for the detection of a virus at regular intervals for the following six months. They found that their infection model led to viremia - viruses in the blood - in all patients, as well as rash and reversible neutropenia in some, which is a decline in a kind of white blood cell. No severe disease was seen in any patients. With the model established, she then described how it has been used to evaluate the efficacy of a live attenuated tetravalent dengue vaccine developed by the NIH and determine which formulation should move forward to late-stage clinical trials. "Back in 2015, there was a live attenuated tetravalent dengue vaccine that was produced by Sanofi-Pasteur that induced what would be considered to be very good neutralizing antibody titers against all four viruses, but the vaccine failed to protect against dengue," she said. "That told us that neutralizing antibody is not necessarily predictive of protection, and that's again one of the reasons that we developed this challenge model." Using their model, Durbin's lab found that one of the vaccine formulations led to 100% protection against viremia and laid the groundwork for the recent licensing of a dengue vaccine in Brazil. This vaccine has now been approved for stage 3 clinical trials in multiple other countries, including the United States. She went on to share more projects done using the dengue CHIM. This included a clinical trial she claimed was her favorite from her work, which showed that a tetravalent vaccine which includes all four dengue subtypes - as opposed to a trivalent vaccine which only includes three subtypes - is necessary to protect people from dengue infection. She ended the talk with some of the work the lab has done setting up a CHIM for Zika virus since 2016. "We weren't sure that we would have enough [cases] really to understand the clinical manifestations of Zika as well as the kinetics of viral replication and shedding," she said. "We also thought it could be very useful for the evaluation of a Zika vaccine given that, again, the outbreak waned very quickly and now we continue to see small outbreaks of Zika, but it's unpredictable when and where they will occur." Durbin closed by acknowledging some of the future work she hopes to do using the Zika human challenge model, emphasizing the usefulness of CHIMs in getting therapeutics approved and understanding how viruses replicate within humans.

articles.title: Superconducting vortices provide experimental evidence that clogging is a phase transition
articles.description: Clogging is a phenomenon in which moving particles get stuck, slowing or blocking the flow, but how this transition occurs has remained experimentally unproven. Researchers from Science Tokyo studied superconducting vortices to demonstrate that clogging is a nonequilibrium phase transition. Using a two-step measurement protocol, they distinguished clogging from conventional pinning and revealed that both transitions share a critical point, offering new insights into predicting and controlling clogging across diverse systems.

articles.title: Today in history, November 24
Two skulls likely belonging to enslaved people returned to Brazil after Harvard used them in eugenics studies
articles.description: Remains believed to have belonged to Africans or Afro-Brazilians repatriated after being flown back by diplomats Two skulls, including that of a man believed to have taken part in Brazil’s greatest slave revolt but whose remains were taken to the United States and used in racist eugenics studies at Harvard University, were repatriated on Wednesday. The remains had been outside Brazil since the 19th century. One was taken about 190 years ago from Salvador, the capital of the state of Bahia; the other, about 160 years ago, from Rio de Janeiro – and were welcomed back in moving, subdued ceremonies in both cities.
